articles.title: Metro 2039: The First Hands-On Preview
articles.summary: In an age where single-player first-person shooters are slowly going extinct because they only make money for their publisher once while multiplayer live-service shooters vie for our time and attention on a daily basis (and often contain lots of bullsh*t, like microtransactions and/or drawn-out gameplay loops), Metro 2039’s single-player-only craftsmanship and attention to detail after my first few hours with it have me already prepared to call it my favorite first-person shooter in a long time.
articles.body:
Metro 2039, very refreshingly, doesn't hold your hand. It throws you straight into the deep end.

Gameplay variety was fantastic during my 3-4 hour hands-on; I was rarely doing the same thing for very long.

Metro 2039 blew me away with its handcrafted hellscapes, intense combat, and attention to detail.

I’ve spent about 3-4 hours with Metro 2039 so far, and it’s already healing me even as the in-game version of me, dubbed The Stranger in this sequel, struggles to breathe through a gas mask whose filters don’t last long, thus requiring me to craft new ones from items scrounged by scouring every last inch of its post-apocalyptic world as the countdown timer on my wristwatch constantly ticks down, threatening to choke me to death if it hits 0:00. In a real world where AI is being shoved down our throats at every corner, from our emails to the customer service reps we interact with, one of my biggest takeaways from Metro 2039 is that even though it’s an apocalypse-ravaged hellscape, every inch of it is very obviously and very painstakingly handcrafted. This franchise always was, of course; this is nothing new.

But still, there’s just something about the way 2039 is hitting for me at this exact moment in time that I needed. It is a game that neither offers nor tolerates any bullsh*t, and I love it for that because said bullsh*t surrounds us in the real world. Metro does not hold your hand. It regularly keeps your blood pressure somewhere between slightly elevated and spiked, and it makes no apologies for it. Its irradiated world is Hell, and it very convincingly conveys that at all times. And in an age where single-player first-person shooters are slowly going extinct because they only make money for their publisher once while multiplayer live-service shooters vie for our time and attention on a daily basis (and often contain lots of bullsh*t, like microtransactions and/or drawn-out gameplay loops), Metro’s single-player-only craftsmanship and attention to detail after my first few hours with it have me already prepared to call it my favorite first-person shooter in a long time.

If you’ve played Metro before you’ll certainly be right at home, but even if you’re new to this series, it’s easy enough to get up to speed with. In short, everything is lethal, from the mutated monstrosities on the surface to rival survivors who’ve laid claim to the places you need to get through to the very air you breathe. You are almost never, ever “safe” in Metro 2039. The one place you can’t get killed is where my preview build started out in the Sevastopolskaya Metro Station, which is filled with NPCs and shopkeepers. It feels very alive – a stark contrast to the 180 that happens as soon as you grab your backpack and gun and exit the metro and head to the very dead surface.

There, you are completely and utterly alone. Not literally, as there are mutated freaks abound, from giant maneating rats to jumpy beasts that like to keep their distance and fling barbs from their tails at you to oversized mosquitos who like to get right in your face to huge prehistoric-sized crustaceans who emerge from the waters of the sewers. And, as mentioned, there are plenty of other survivors out there too. Except all of them are hostile – or at least, everyone I met outside of the metro during my hands-on time immediately wanted me dead.

I appreciated being thrown straight into the deep end as soon as I reached the surface. Yes, a map on a crude tablet gave me a general idea of where to go towards my next objective, but beyond that I was on my own to figure out the best path – and to survive along the way. I wandered into a drug store – well, the picked-apart remnan ts of one, obviously – and I checked every nook and cranny for crafting items I could use to make medkits, ammo, and most crucially of all, new gas mask filters. Pressing Y on the keyboard lifts your gun up a little higher so you can clearly see your digital wristwatch, which constantly ticks down the minutes and seconds until your current filter will expire.

I found environmental puzzles tucked away in various places, and felt compelled to try and solve them all because the reward would likely be those precious crafting resources that would well and truly keep me alive. Some of these puzzles utilized the Stranger’s UV light, guiding you to follow clues that were scrawled on walls and floors such that they could only be seen under the purple hue. In my experience, these challenges may have been optional, but they were worth pursuing every single time. Again, it can’t be said enough: Metro 2039 does not mess around. It does not waste your time. There doesn’t seem to be any filler content here. Everything seems to be meticulously considered and implemented.

The weapons are something of a puzzle unto themselves. They can all be modified and customized, from their scopes to their hilts to their muzzles and more. At one point fairly early on, I found a double-barrelled sho tgun that I decided to swap out for the single-barrel version I had on me, and it became my go-to gun in the close-quarters “dungeons” I spent much of the latter half of my demo traipsing through. I even found a laser sight to attach to it, which is almost comically pointless on a close-quarters death-dealer like this, but I didn’t have anything better to stick on there, so I figured, “What the heck.”

Oh, and as you may very well have guessed by now, ammo is scarce . You can find and craft different types – everything from rudimentary metal balls to incendiary rounds to armor-piercing machinegun rounds – and you’ll certainly need to. I survived a miniboss fight with a nine-foot-tall mutant and his feral accomplices with so few rounds left on me that I prayed there was nothing else waiting for me for the next little while, because the fight took place in knee-deep sewer water, which meant that I had nowhere I could set my backpack down in order to craft more. (Fortunately, Metro’s game designers took pity on me, and I was indeed given a short reprieve.)

But you also have throwables that help tilt the scales slightly back in your favor. I was quite fond of the knives, as not only can they enable you to stealthily take out regular human enemies without alerting anyone else, but as you’d expect in a game with such stringent resource management, you can retrieve your blades from the corpses of your targets (or the ground if you happen to miss a throw). But as the caliber of foe ramped up as I progressed, the Molotov cocktails started to get a lot more useful.

Adding to the list of things I love about Metro 2039 so far is its gameplay variety. I was never doing the same thing for very long during my few hours with it, and I applaud it for that. As I mentioned, I started with a rare moment of safety in the metro station before moving topside and having plenty of room to roam while contending with the mutated bestiary I talked about earlier. And as I progressed, I was kept on my toes with a number of different gameplay scenarios.

At one point, I was conveniently left a scoped rifle on the decaying second-story balcony of a building adjacent to a nest of Novoreich members – they’re the bad-guy faction here, under the direction of Fuhrer Hunter, who was only teased in my demo, so I can’t really determine much about the quality of him as a foe, besides the fact that he is very obviously a post-apocalyptic Hitler and therefore I’ll take great pleasure in gunning him and everyone in his ranks down in the final game. Sadly I don’t have any footage of this to show you.

Anyway, I picked up that scoped rifle and started loudly picking off Novoreich scum – they told on themselves by having bright lights attached to their weapons, making things easier for me. Later, in a completely different scenario, I found myself in an abandoned da ycare, where my electronics got jammed in one particularly creepy room, making my skin crawl despite there being nary a living creature around and motivating me to want to get the heck out of there as quickly as possible.

Thankfully, you do get a break from the constant juggling act of crafting and installing new gas mask filters in Metro’s subterranean “dungeons,” at least. The air is clean enough in these to be able to safely remove your gas mask, and in the several I battled through, all favored close-quarters combat, which made me all-too-happy to bust out that double-barrelled shotgun I’d picked up early on. In one of them, I was able to choke out the only upstairs guard without alerting anyone below, and he was conveniently standing (well, slouching now) next to an open air duct that let me creep down silently and in the shadows to the dark main base below, which was teeming with unfriendly humans. I botched my stealth attempt here trying to thread the needle with a thrown knife at a tough angle, and I got discovered. It then became an old-fashioned shootout, in which I was happy to break out Metro’s lean feature from behind cover to expose as little of my body to the baddies as possible.

This was the story of my hands-on time: combat encounters came in many different forms, shapes, and sizes, and I really appreciated that.

Speaking of appreciation, it will come as no surprise to anyone that’s played a Metro game before that 2039 is, visually speaking, gorgeous. It’s bleak and horrifying, of course, but it’s rendered beautifully. Developer 4A Games’ (read our new interview with them about how Russia's invasion of Ukraine changed their development approach) proprietary engine is really cooking here, though I should confess that framerate isn’t something I can reasonably report on right now – not just because I was playing a preview build of a game that won’t be out for six months, but also because I was playing it remotely via GeForce Now. So we’ll have to see how it holds up once I can throw my own 5080 at it, rather than the 5080 that was feeding the game to me via the cloud.

I’ve come this far in this preview and I still feel like I’ve barely scratched the surface of what Metro 2039 is offering. Series veterans have no dou bt already been nodding their heads along in satisfaction, while those new to Metro are in for a treat – if the few hours I got to play are any indication. February 2027 was already looking stacked with the first big wave of post-GTA 6 releases, but Metro 2039 just cemented itself on my must-play list for that crowded month.

While you're here, check out these previews of other big upcoming games we've played recently!

Ryan McCaffrey is IGN's executive editor of previews and host of IGN's weekly Xbox show, Podcast Unlocked , and a co-host of Next-Gen Console Watch . He's a North Jersey guy, so it's "Taylor ham," not "pork roll." Debate it with him on Twitter at @DMC_Ryan .

articles.title: Metro 2039 Developers on How Russia's Invasion of Ukraine Changed Their Plans
articles.summary: After finishing the four-or-so-hour preview build of Metro 2039, the upcoming first-person shooter sequel from Ukrainian developer 4A Games and falling completely in love with it, I reached out to the team to ask some questions about how they've approached the latest entry in their post-apocalyptic franchise – both in terms of the game itself, but also because their real lives have changed so much since Russia's invasion of their country in 2022.
articles.body:
After finishing the four-or-so-hour preview build of Metro 2039, the upcoming first-person shooter sequel from Ukrainian developer 4A Games and falling completely in love with it , I reached out to the team to ask some questions about how they've approached the latest entry in their post-apocalyptic franchise – both in terms of the game itself, but also in terms of how their real lives have changed since Russia's invasion of their country in 2022.

"First of all, it's impacted the team," said creative director Andriy "MLS" Shevchenko. "The world changes the team completely, their way of being, their way of thinking, and their way of understanding what's going on in general. So automatically it brings new visions and new philosophy into the game through the team. And everything else is just details. Story changed? Yes. Some gameplay elements changed? Yes. But first of all, it's the team."

"And I would say that effect on the team did actually directly affect the story in the way that previous Metro games were about the prevention of war," said executive producer Jon Bloch. "And when Russia started its full-scale invasion of Ukraine, it brought war to our doorsteps and we had to change our approach about what kind of story we wanted to tell. We wanted to tell now the consequences of war, what happens when war comes to you. And so it was a pretty major change to what we were doing. We had to try to see from a production standpoint what we could save and what needed to change. We tried to save as much as we could, but quite a lot of our plans changed overnight."

"Yeah, that's true," added co-creative director and audio lead Pavel Ulmer. "And the very Metro franchise, its very nature just became too close to reality. So the perception changed dramatically. Basically, it's all divided from before and after."

Pivoting to the game itself, I asked what lessons they've taken from previous Metro games and applied to 2039. "Avoid empty spaces," Shevchenko said. "The density of everything, it's our goal and the thing to be proud of now." Bloch added: "To that last question, to that last answer, density is a big one. Density of objects, density of sound, density of animation, density of characters, density of everything, density of detail. We rebuilt our render from the ground up to be fully ray traced and really push forward on the realistic picture that we can provide and the amount of assets that we can put into the world, the amount of dynamic things that we can put into the world, and all of that while still retaining performance and running on all platforms. The engine from day one has always been multi-platform. So performance is a huge, huge factor for us. But a lot of the things that we did were with the goal of increasing the amount of stuff that we can do, giving our designers and our artists more freedom, taking away a lot of the barriers that they have to be able to do what they want while still retaining performance."

"So basically our goal is not to make the area cool only where the cut scene is supposed to be, you know, but to make all the areas look cool and nice and natural, believable," Ulmer noted.

Finally, I asked the Metro team what tips they'd give to new players for whom Metro 2039 will be their first game in the series. "Do not be afraid to explore," Shevchenko suggested. "Explore and you will find a lot of interesting things." Ulmer added, "Do not rush," before Bloch chimed in: "Metro is a slow burn. It's not fast-paced. We have fast-paced action sequences, but overall, it's something you sit and absorb. You spend the time to learn about the story, the atmosphere, everything. And it's something for people who want to observe and to think, to question things. It's something we hope is more meaningful."

"For our younger audience, I might say, use sprint only when you really have to," Ulmer suggested. "Don't sprint through the game all over the place. There's a lot of things to enjoy, as Jon mentioned, a lot of things to hear, to think about, just to absorb the atmosphere. So sprint only when you actually have to sprint, running from a lot of threats that will try to chase you. In that case, go for it. But it's like a good movie. Playing this story just in order to finish, it's a bad idea. Enjoy it. Take your time."

Ryan McCaffrey is IGN's executive editor of previews and host of IGN's weekly Xbox show, Podcast Unlocked , and a co-host of Next-Gen Console Watch . He's a North Jersey guy, so it's "Taylor ham," not "pork roll." Debate it with him on Twitter at @DMC_Ryan .

articles.title: Wilderings: The Lost Spring Gameplay Trailer Reveals Volcanic Biome, a Moth Boss, and a Version 1.0 Release Window
articles.body:
At gamescom 2026, Kabam and Herobeat Studios revealed a brand-new gameplay trailer for Wilderings that unveiled a fiery new Volcanic biome, a first look at Röhe the Moth Boss, and the confirmation that the open-world action-adventure game will be launching its Version 1.0 update in spring 2027.

Wilderings, which also encourages exploration and features fast-paced action, roguelite progression, and creature collecting, follows Abi and her companion Rif as they traverse a fractured world that is quickly being consumed by darkness.

To help in her journey, she will discover and adopt mysterious creatures known as Hântu, which she can use to help her fight, get through tough spots with their abilities, and to move about the world. In this new Volcanic biome, Abi will run into at least three Hântu, Razzle (explosive projectiles that burn and multiply), Mokul (summons pyroclastic rain that scorches an area), and Furioso (throws magma that spreads between enemies).

As for Röhe, this Moth Boss is actually a young hunter from the Frostlands who will challenge Abi in this new region. To make it through the test set in a "magma-lit arena," Abi will have to perfet her movement, combat skills, and Hântu abilities.

For those at gamescom, Wilderings: The Lost Spring will be available to play at the Indie Arena Booth, Hall 10.2 Booth F010g - E019, from August 26-30.

For more, check out everything announced from Opening Night Live and what else to expect from the rest of gamescom.

articles.title: Heroes of Might and Magic 3 Remake Preview: Hands-On with Ubisoft’s Reborn Strategy Classic - Gamescom 2026
articles.summary: In a year where Ubisoft announced and shipped the Assassin’s Creed: Black Flag remake, a revival of Heroes of Might and Magic 3 might not be the highest-profile remake project, but it’s an appreciated one nevertheless. While the announcement did not mince words about the scope and scale of the project — the 1999 title is being brought back to life for both PC and consoles — IGN got to go hands on with the game in a remote session to see how this version compares to the nearly three-decades-old original.
articles.body:
The graphics are entirely new, but the underlying classic gameplay has been preserved.

The UI has also being redone, bringing it up to modern standards from its MS-DOS-era origins.

The remake awesomely supports all of the old original and community-made maps.

In a year where Ubisoft announced and shipped the Assassin’s Creed: Black Flag remake, a revival of Heroes of Might and Magic 3 might not be the highest-profile remake project, but it’s an appreciated one nevertheless. While the announcement did not mince words about the scope and scale of the project — the 1999 title is being brought back to life for both PC and consoles — IGN got to go hands on with the game in a remote session to see how this version compares to the nearly three-decades-old original.

For the uninitiated, Heroes of Might and Magic is a strategy game series where players take on the roles of factions that guide armies into battles on an overworld map. Each faction, led by a Hero, explores a map with multiple points of interest, recruiting new soldiers, gaining resources, and eventually clashing with enemy troops. In those clashes, players move their units around a side-view battlefield broken into hexagonal panels and fight to be the last group standing for their hero.

All this gameplay is intact in the remake, making Heroes of Might and Magic III feel like the classic that fans have known and loved over the last few decades with a new coat of paint. Though Heroes of Might and Magic III was remastered by Ubisoft a decade ago, the 2026 title is a true top-to-bottom remake of the game in terms of visuals, while leaving the gameplay relatively untouched.

The modern 3D graphics are bolstered by a modern user interface revamp that does not entirely ditch the MS-DOS look of the classic games but instead evokes them as the foundation for new art and menus to be built upon. That is to say, the remake does not throw away what fans liked about the earlier game, but definitely tries to make things more readable. There is nowhere this is more obvious than the base-building screen, where the brand-new art no longer has you scanning the screen for the window of the base you’re looking to upgrade, and is at a glance more easy to see and decode for people who have not memorized the layout yet.

Heroes of Might and Magic 3 Remake Screenshots

In the demo, we were given access to two different maps. The first, a campaign tutorial map titled The Queen’s Departure, teaches players about the basics of Heroes of Might and Magic III’s core systems of movement and battle through the story of a queen leaving her kingdom after her father’s death. She and her retinue battle back bandits on the way to the port, but it’s the surprise attack from demons that truly catches her party off guard.

The other map, Arrogance, is a classic scenario from the original game separate from the campaign that has gained a well-loved reputation among fans. This map has multiple factions warring over a number of towns and shipyards for supremacy in the region. The map design discourages rushing with its layout and lets players dive into subterranean layers for resources, so it has remained popular due to its complexity and variation.

While it is somewhat accurate to say that Heroes of Might and Magic III is being brought back from the dead, it is also worth acknowledging that it has never really disappeared. A dedicated community of players has been playing and creating maps for it for a quarter-century, and Ubisoft says that the company has been involving key members of the community in the creation of the remake.

The reason that bears mentioning is that Heroes of Might and Magic III Remake supports all those old maps from the jump, letting maps like Arrogance live again in 2026. The remake scans the topography and design of the original maps, both from the campaign and from fans, and recreates it in 3D with modern graphics. The map and campaign editors will ship with HOMM3R at release.

Within Arrogance, I managed to — true to its name — work myself into scenarios where I thought I was winning only to be rightfully cowed by enemy armies. On my first try, I was too slow to deal with some enemy monsters guarding a nearby castle town, and by the time I finally cleared the way and took over the town, a rival kingdom had already built ships and invaded my coast. My units were not nearly strong enough to take them on and I had to slowly watch while they took over every resource on the way to eliminating my faction from the map.

The second time around, speed was my aspiration, so I used a faction of mages to build and expand as fast as humanly possible. This plan worked better, at least until a nearby contingent of Griffins ran roughshod over my units, leaving me vulnerable to enemies until I retreated into an underground lair of the undead. The demo ended before I could find out what backing myself into this particular pincer attack would earn me, but maybe that’s for the best.

Between the various efforts to bring Heroes of Might and Magic to modern audiences and this latest remake to bridge the gap with classic fans, it is a good time to be an enthusiast of the strategy series. With Heroes of Might and Magic III coming to consoles, perhaps it will also find a new audience of players who will discover what players in 1999 and since have known all along: that this has always been a fantastic strategy series.

articles.title: Atari Is Re-Releasing 39 Atari 2600 Games on Working, Physical Cartridges
articles.summary: Atari has today announced a new physical game collaboration with Activision called the Atari x Activision Collection, reuniting Activision with Atari after almost 50 years.
articles.body:
Atari has today announced a new physical game collaboration with Activision called the Atari x Activision Collection. The unexpected project reunites Activision with Atari after almost 50 years.

The full set of working, physical game cartridges includes 39 classic Activision games, like Pitfall!, River Raid, and Kaboom!, and there will be three ways to purchase them.

Individual, “Standard Edition” versions of 12 of the games will be available from November for USD$35 each. The 12 games include Pitfall!, River Raid, Megamania, Enduro, Kaboom!, H.E.R.O., Pressure Cooker, Private Eye, River Raid II, Keystone Kapers, The Activision Decathlon, and Pitfall II: Lost Caverns (although Atari notes The Activision Decathlon and Pitfall II: Lost Caverns will actually ship at a later date than the other titles). The Standard Edition games feature full packaging and a printed, colour manual inspired by the original releases. They’ll be compatible with Atari 2600+ and Atari 7800+ consoles, as well as original Atari 2600 and 7800 hardware.

There will also be four box sets available, which will widen the collection to the full 39 games. The first of the four box sets (which are dubbed Treasure, Speed, Secrets, and Victory) will be available from late November, with the remaining three will follow over the first three quarters of 2027. These will be available via pre-orders at atari.com for USD$250. A complete collection of all 39 games (which will reportedly include a yet-to-be-announced “collectible item”) will also be sold via pre-order for USD$1000.

“In 1979, a group of Atari programmers set out to prove that great games could come from independent creators and ended up changing the industry forever,” said Atari’s VP of hardware Matt Burnett in a comment published in conjunction with today’s announcement. “The Atari x Activision Collection brings that legacy to life through the games themselves, giving fans an opportunity to experience, collect and preserve the work of the developers who helped establish a new model for the video game industry.”

The resurrection of fresh, physical versions of Activision’s very oldest games comes as an interesting surprise amid the bleak times collectors of physical media are currently otherwise facing , and with PlayStation maintaining its decision to discontinue physical discs in the near future won’t have any negative impact on its business either now or in the future.

Luke is a Senior Editor on the IGN reviews team. You can track him down on Bluesky @mrlukereilly to ask him things about stuff.

articles.title: Total War: Warhammer 40k – The First Hands-On Preview - Gamescom 2026
articles.summary: The core of Total War’s DNA appears intact so far in Total War: Warhammer 40K, but we will have to wait and see if the heavier focus on ranged combat and the other 40k influence will result in something genuinely special or a creation that has fallen to Chaos.
articles.body:
The setting has jumped way into the future

Customization for units is a welcome addition, though it's a bit bare-bones at the moment.

Ever since Creative Assembly released the first Total War: Warhammer back in 2016, the part of the community more interested in its futuristic sibling has been clamoring for a version set in the 41st Millennium of the long-running tabletop miniatures series. It may have taken longer than folks would have liked, but Total War: Warhammer 40K is on the horizon, and during a recent event, I had a chance to go hands-on with an early build of the strategy sequel, purging some savage Orks and spreading the word of the God Emperor. The build I got to try consisted of three focused slices – a tutorial, a tease of how the campaign will play out (including some customization goodness), and finally a massive battle – all of which were seen through the helmets of the Space Marines. All things told, it was about an hour of explosions, bullets, and little dudes shouting “For the Emperor!”

Up until now, the Total War series, while featuring ranged units, has been about two armies getting up close and slashing and stabbing one another with swords and the like. Not only does this latest entry mark the first run with Creative Assembly's new engine, WarCore, but also the first ranged-focused title in the long-running franchise. Trebuchets are out, and tanks and walking mechs are in. With this massive leap forward in time to the 41st millennium, gameplay itself has had to catch up and evolve a bit.

Playing through the tutorial, I got a very basic understanding of how this beloved franchise will operate in this new grimdark setting. My squad was sent in to secure the crash site, giving me a crash course on how to move around, get to cover, and more fun things like raining missiles down on the greenskins. It also proved a great opportunity to start getting a grasp of some of the new mechanics that players will have to master when it eventually releases, such as strafe-firing, suppressing enemies, and calling down drop pods from orbit with fresh forces. Perhaps my favorite of these is that there wasn’t a single ammo bar anywhere to be seen. Thank the Emperor.

Even with all the guns, you don’t have to worry about 40k losing the intense close-combat brawls, as that is still here too. The best showcase of what the new WarCore engine will offer became most apparent when I would pause the action and zoom into the large marine-on-ork bloodbaths, seeing all of the different units covered in blood or mid-vault over a piece of cover. Seeing my Space Marines’ chainswords and their motorized teeth sparking against the axes of the Orks while the bullets shot overhead was a sight to behold.

While this latest iteration certainly looks to change things up a bit, Total War 40k is still very much a Total War game, with that same tactically rich strategic playground the series is known for. Even in that introductory scenario, between the sheer number of bodies fighting and all the fronts of the skirmish I had to manage kept me on my toes. Positioning and countering enemies remains something you will always need to consider, with this newest entry looking to offer even more ways to conquer and twist the battlefield to your needs. Lessons that, being a bit out of practice with the Total War series, I was reminded of during a rather tense moment during the campaign mission I got to try.

The mission in question was for me to go in and retake the nearby Thetha-Citadel Astropathic Relay Station and get rid of the xeno threat, which was once again the orks, whose space force was already positioned and laying waste to the planet not just from the ground, but from orbit as well. Before heading down to the ground myself, I wanted to take a peek around the system that my Space Marines found themselves in. Planets orbited a menacing blood red star with what looks to be an equally imposing Chaos Ga te looming nearby. I couldn’t interact with them or utilize them in any way during the demo; they simply teased at mechanics to come.

Zooming back into the planet I was tasked to clear, I was greeted with a more familiar Total War screen, with various zones, cities, and my armies to command. I could easily rotate my view around large swaths of the planet to find my objective, and the view of space behind the curved world lent itself really well to the sense of scale this game will have. After training up some new troops and making my way to the station, it was time for my Immortals of Demos (the custom chapter I set up and colored before this mission) to deal with Snaz Braggerz and cleanse the citadel.

Fielding some squads of Aggressor marines, Intercessors, Dreadnoughts, Repulsor Executioner tanks and more, I assigned them to groups and sent them on their way. After some poor battlefield decisions by yours truly (note to self: don’t spread yourself too thinly and forget to turn the speed back down when things get hairy), the orks quickly began marching towards my last group of marines and tanks, which I had earlier in the match hunkered down and held the high ground of a nearby landing pad. After a few tense minutes of exchanging gunfire and calling down ordnance from my ships in orbit, we managed to rout the orks and destroy their Stompa super-heavy walker. Watching the yellow monstrosity tip over and explode was nearly as rewarding to see as when I managed to do so while playing the actual tabletop version of 40k. The Imperium of Man had come out victorious once again! Unfortunately, this sense of accomplishment and boost to my ego carried me straight into the “Very hard” big battle that Creative Assembly had also left us to check out if we wanted, and let’s just say things didn’t go quite so well…

Now, a moment ago, you may have caught me mentioning my “Immortals of Demos,” my custom chapter of Space Marines I got to color up before the mission. Customization is a big part of 40K, and miniature games in general, so I was glad that right at the start of the campaign slice of my demo, I got to check out an early look at what to expect in this regard. For those who have never dabbled in the realm of tabletop miniature games, most of the time, the armies you bring to the table have to be built first, and normally also all come unpainted. The “grey pile of shame” is a hobbyist term we use to lovingly refer to all the models in our backlog that we have yet to paint and customize.

The offerings at this stage were admittedly a bit lacking, with only a base, accents, and detail colors able to be adjusted and applied to the whole armor, in addition to customizing your chapter's name and emblem. The number of colors available to pick from, however, was pretty impressive, with Creative Assembly using the actual paint colors Games Workshop releases. Poking through the options, I saw the familiar Caledor Sky and Screamer Pink before settling on Mournfang Brown for the base of my Immortals of Demos. The representative on site, though, did make it clear that there would be far more options and details for players to explore when 40k eventually ships. As someone with a rather large pile of grey unpainted units (but they’re primed, I swear!), I hope one of those options includes letting me make my armies in that signature plastic look. In all seriousness though, I do hope that the customization offers enough flexibility that physical 40k players will be able to recreate some of their custom paint jobs here in Total War. I don’t want to just play Space Marines, I want to command MY Space Marines.

The team at Creative Assembly has a lot to prove with Total War: Warhammer 40k after various issues and missteps with how DLC has been handled with Total War: Warhammer III and 2023’s Total War: Pharaoh. What I saw during the preview event shows promise; since the community has been asking for this, I’m hoping they can deliver.

Total War: Warhammer 40k still has a ways to go before it launches, with no current release window set. We haven’t seen a peep out of the Aeldari faction yet, and so far we’ve only had teases and glimpses at the real depth that Creative Assembly is putting into this latest tactical titan. The core of Total War’s DNA appears intact so far, but we will have to wait and see if the heavier focus on ranged combat and the other 40k influence will result in something genuinely special or a creation that has fallen to Chaos.

articles.title: Persona 4 Revival: The Good and the Bad of Our First Hands-On – Gamescom 2026
articles.summary: In the pantheon of the Persona series, its fourth entry is held in high regard, and time will tell if Persona 4 Revival will prove to be the best of the bunch. The little bit I got to see is at least making it a pretty strong contender for that award, and it still very much feels like Persona 4. But anyone who has played it before knows it’s a very long game, so we will have to wait and see whether it's worth tuning in for or changing the channel.
articles.body:
A new breadcrumb trail that leads you to your next quest or objective is a nice accessibility feature, but we hope there's an option to turn it off for players already familiar with Persona 4.

The big new combat feature in Revival comes in the form of “Prime Time,” a sort of super-mode that you can activate after filling a special bar.

The new voice acting is a bit of an adjustment, but we liked what/who we heard.

Last year’s Persona 3 Reload was a modern revamp of the game that wound up defining the core pillars of what the Persona would become. P3 Reload proved that Atlus could modernize its older Persona titles while maintaining its feel and identity, and now it’s Persona 4’s turn with Persona 4 Revival. Based on the PlayStation Vita’s enhanced “Golden” version of the game, Revival will once again see your small group of Persona users figure out the cause of a mysterious set of disappearances and murders taking place in the small town of Inaba, Japan. The demo I checked out dropped me into a few different points set during the early hours of the story, letting me get a sampling of the story, along with a taste of the new anime cutscenes from MAPPA (the same studio that did Persona 5 Royal’s opening), take on some Shadows, and even do a little exploring around Inaba. It’s been a while since I last visited the foggy town, and I was excited to check in and see how this new take on the RPG had changed things up.

I opted to start my time with Revival getting straight into the action and exploring Yukiko’s castle.

The dungeon felt largely as I remembered it from Persona 4 and Golden. The structure remains, consisting of tight hallways with rooms containing chests and shadows that direct you towards the boss room. New to this version was a sort of pathing graphic, resembling something like fairy dust pointing me where to go. I’m not sure if this was something strictly added to this demo to help me see content with the short time we had or if it is a feature that will be present in the Revival’s final release, but I hope that you can turn it off. I’ve always felt like the mini-maps in Persona 3 through 5 do a good job in keeping me from getting lost, so having a constantly-on breadcrumb trail telling me where to go feels a bit unnecessary. I’m fine with the assistance being in the game, I just would have an issue if it is always active. It’d be like having Teddie constantly talking to you with no way to get him to shut up.

But what would a dungeon be without some baddies getting in your way and trying to take you out, and this is where I’m reminded that I have always been a fan of the modern Persona’s combat system. Revival adopts and brings over a very similar system to last year's Persona 3 Reload, which adapted some of the intricacies from Persona 5, which itself was expanded from the original 3 and 4 releases. The big bombastic notices when you hit an enemy’s weakness, knocking them down, the impressive all-out team attacks, and Persona 4 Golden’s approach to Shuffle Time (the post-combat selection that can net you new personas for the main character and other goodies to pick from) all return in the new remake. That said, Revival still has some new twists to look forward to as well.

The big new combat feature in Revival comes in the form of “Prime Time.” Think of it as a sort of super-mode that you can activate after filling a special bar. Prime Time gives a character three back-to-back turns where all the costs for their skills and spells are reduced to zero, while also granting you access to a dramatic all-target special attack. You fill the bar by performing actions and taking damage, with things like hitting an enemy’s weakness filling more of the bar, making the whole thing feel a bit like Revival’s take on a Limit Break system. The demo had the Prime Time bar filling really quickly, just to give me a chance to check it out, even letting me get multiple triggers of it during a single fight if I wanted to, and I was promised that, come release, this powerful tool wouldn’t be something you could just bring out quite so willy-nilly as in this specific build. That said, I can only start to imagine just how powerful this will get when I start having personas with higher-level skills - a full stack of debuffs or buffs using Debilitate or Heat Riser for free and done all at once or hitting three Brave Blades without the health loss? Um, yes please! One caveat is that while in Prime Time you lose access to using the All-Out Attack if you knock down all enemies. It’s a small price to pay for something so strong, and I’m curious to see how well Revival manages to balance this new Prime Time mechanic, as it feels like it is balancing on a knife's edge and could easily slip into making many of the more challenging fights feel more trivial.

Baton Pass also makes its Persona 4 debut, the nifty feature that allows you to switch to another party member if you strike an enemy’s weakness. First introduced in Persona 5, and with Persona 3 Reload incorporating a similar system with “Shifting,” it’s a powerful tool that has already proven its worth in previous titles, and it’s a welcome addition to Revival. Because of the demo taking place so early in the game, I really didn’t notice much else in the way of differences in how battles played out, which I’m perfectly happy with, since Persona 4 already had such a solid system to begin with!

My time wasn’t spent just taking out shadows, though, as I got to do some light exploring around Inaba itself. Well, at least as much as you really can do at that point in the story, as most stores are all closed or or had some other given reason preventing me from going inside. I got to visit Igor and crew in the Velvet Room, fuse some Personas, and even start Marie’s Social Link. It felt good getting to check out the old stomping grounds like Junes and the Samegawa, and I even spotted a little Easter egg (I was told I was the first one to notice it during the event) of Kyouji Kuzunoha, a devil summoner and the (sort-of) protagonist of Megami Tensei: Devil Summoner, which released on the Sega Saturn and PSP. I can’t wait to walk around this new Inaba more and see what other goodies there are to discover.

Meanwhile, Revival features brand-new voice actors for the cast alongside rerecorded music tracks, which will take some time to get used to. Seeing Yosuke’s portrait talking and not hearing Yuri Lowenthal’s voice coming out, even knowing it was coming, took me by surprise a bit. While I only got a very small sampling of the voice acting and new versions of the soundtrack, everything I heard, such as Yosuke’s new actor Paul Castro Jr., was well done. It will take me a bit to adjust to all of the new actors and tunes in Revival, but I’m curious to hear how the full soundtrack and rest of the cast come out.

From a visual standpoint, Revival is definitely a step up from the vanilla and Golden releases of Persona 4, but I’m not sold on all of the changes. The new character models all look fantastic and are definitely up to the same quality as those in P3 Reload and Persona 5, but I find that the character portraits themselves lack some depth and shading. The battle portraits for the cast feel like a bit of a downgrade as well. In the previous editions, these were larger and colored on the side of the screen, while Revival’s are pretty small and black and white, with the only color seeming to be the character’s hair, and only when you are giving them commands.

Persona 3 and its follow-up, Persona 3 FES, when released on the PS2, shone the light on the series and got a lot of eyes looking in its direction, but Persona 4 is where the series really started bringing in the fans. That growth continues on with the Persona series as a whole, with the franchise recently surpassing 30 million copies sold. 2027 is setting itself up as a really good year for fans of RPGs, and Persona 4 Revival will be leading the pack when it releases in February. I’m hopeful that things like the glowing objective trail being toggleable or some tweaks to the portraits and UI will be included, and I’m perhaps the most intrigued to see how Atlus manages to balance Prime Time during late game.

In the pantheon of the Persona series, its fourth entry is held in high regard, and time will tell if this third iteration will prove to be the best of the bunch. The little bit I got to see is at least making it a pretty strong contender for that award, and it still very much feels like Persona 4. But anyone who has played it before knows it’s a very long game, so we will have to wait and see whether it's worth tuning in for or changing the channel.

articles.title: LEGO Super Mario Minifigure Sets Unveiled, Including Bowser's Castle and Mario Kart
articles.summary: LEGO has finally revealed its Super Mario range that will include minifigures for the first time, including playsets for Bowser's Castle and numerous Mario Kart vehicles.
articles.body:
LEGO has finally revealed its Super Mario range that will include minifigures for the first time, including playsets for Bowser's Castle and numerous Mario Kart vehicles.

Super Mario has been appearing in LEGO sets for years, though mostly as part of the company's bigger-scale range designed to work with the interactive Super Mario toy unit.

That experiment now seems to over, however, with the long-awaited rollout of Super Mario sets scaled to minifigure size. And indeed, these will also include a growing range of Mario minifigures, with Luigi, Peach, Toad, Yoshi, Koopa Troopa, and Bowser Jr. all glimpsed in this first wave, as well as a Bowser big fig. The range will all be available from January 1, 2027.

Mario's Pipe Jump (72052) – 61 pieces, $9.99

Racing with Mario (72054) – 84 pieces, $14.99

Mario's Beach Adventures (72055) – 196 pieces, $19.99

Luigi & Bowser Jr.'s Race (72056) – 104 pieces, $29.99

Yoshi at Mario's House (72057) – 147 pieces, $39.99

Bowser's Rumbling Race (72058) – 409 pieces, $59.99

Fire Mario & Bowser's Castle (72060) – 850 pieces, $99.99

Fire Luigi vs. Koopa Troopa Battle (72061) – 241 pieces, $29.99

The range begins with Mario's Pipe Jump (72052), a 61-piece set priced at $9.99 that features a Mario minifigure, dinky Goomba element and large green warp pipe. Next up is Racing with Mario (72054), an 84-piece set for $14.99 that features a Mario minifigure and the plumber's classic kart. Green and red shells are also included, as is a banana.

Mario's Beach Adventures (72055) sees the hero take some downtime by the sea. This 196-piece set sells for $19.99 and includes a Mario in swim trunks minifigure (no, he doesn't have nipples), plus a buildable snack bar, lounger and giant enemy crab.

Luigi & Bowser Jr.'s Race (72056) is essentially a larger version of the previous Racing with Mario set, except with both Luigi and Bowser Jr. Both characters are included as minifigures, alongside their karts and accessories. This is a 104-piece set that will sell for $29.99.

Moving onto the slightly bigger sets, Yoshi at Mario's House (72057) is a 147-piece build that sells for $39.99. Included here are Mario and a slightly awkward-looking Yoshi minifigure, plus a goomba.

Bowser's Rumbling Race (72058) is another Mario Kart set, this time with 409 pieces for $59.99. Here, you can expand your starting lineup with karts for Toad, Bowser, Goomba and Mario Kart World's fan-favorite Cow. The first two characters are minifigures, while the latter is a buildable design.

The biggest set in this starting wave is Fire Mario & Bowser's Castle, which will weigh in at 850 pieces and sell for $99.99. This features Fire Mario, Peach and Koopa Trooper minifigures, the Bowser big fig and a goomba. It's a cool-looking design, even if LEGO is clearly making us wait for the Peach's Castle set we all really want.

Lastly, Fire Luigi vs. Koopa Troopa Battle (72061) is a smaller 241-piece set featuring, unsurprisingly, Fire Luigi and a Koopa Troopa minifigures.

"The new LEGO minifigures mark a refreshed LEGO Super Mario theme, newly centred on creative LEGO minifigure roleplay action," LEGO stated in a press release today. "The refresh of the Super Mario theme will see building experiences arriving for LEGO Super Mario centred on creative LEGO minifigure roleplay, featuring iconic characters, karts, and environments from the Super Mario and Mario Kart universe."

articles.title: Xbox and IKEA Furniture Collaboration Includes Thumbstick Stools, Tables, and D-Pad Accessories
articles.summary: IKEA has unveiled a range of official Xbox furniture, including gaming chairs, display stands and cozy-looking D-pad cushion.
articles.body:
IKEA has unveiled a range of official Xbox furniture, including gaming chairs, display stands and cozy-looking D-pad cushions.

The range goes on sale in the U.K. from October via the retailer's website and in IKEA stores, and is officially named "YXSTABY" — a name I won't try and pronounce out loud.

In a press release sent to IGN today, IKEA said that YXSTABY reflected "an era where gaming furniture is moving out of teen bedrooms and man caves and into the mainstream living room."

Created together by Xbox and IKEA designers, the nine-piece collection includes functional furniture such as controller display boxes, TV stands on castors, and a side table to store all your gaming accessories.

Xbox and IKEA Furniture Collaboration Photos

There are also more bizarre-looking additions, such as green and black "gaming Thumbstick stools", which really do look like the sticks of an Xbox controller at giant size. IKEA says these were developed using the controller's original 3D design files for maximum authenticity. It even tilts as you lean, echoing the thumbstick's motion to keep gamers "comfortably engaged during intense sessions."

My favorite item is probably the green gaming D-pad cushion, although I do also rather like the D-pad platter, themed after the concave metal D-pad on Xbox Elite pads.

"At Xbox, we think a lot about what helps players feel immersed in a game," said Carl Ledbetter, Xbox Head of Design. "The hardware is an important part of that, but so is the world you create around it. Working with IKEA gave us the opportunity to design for the entire gaming experience at home, from the screen to the space around it."

The range is currently on display on Xbox's booth over at Gamescom, ahead of its wider launch in a couple of months. Tempted? You could be leaning forward on your thumbstick stool just in time for GTA 6 , or settling down on your D-pad cushion waiting for Fable .

articles.title: Ikea’s Xbox collection includes a giant thumbstick stool
articles.summary: Ikea has teamed up with Microsoft to launch a new assortment of Xbox-inspired furniture and home accessories.
articles.body: Ikea has teamed up with Microsoft to launch a new assortment of gaming-inspired furniture and home accessories, coinciding with the 25th anniversary of the first Xbox console. The nine-piece Yxstaby collection (good luck pronouncing that) includes a TV stand, laptop stand, side table, lounge chair, and multi-functional toolbox, with standout products like a stool, cushion, decorative platter, and mirrored display box being specifically designed around recognizable Xbox controller motifs. The Yxstaby range makes it easier to “bring play into a room and tuck everything away afterwards,” according to Ikea’s press release, with each piece created as a collaboration between Xbox and Ikea designers to naturally co-exist alongside the furniture you already own. It makes use of familiar Scandi-themes like neutral colors and shapes, paired with flashes of Xbox’s iconic green that draw attention to the pockets and compartments designed to hold gaming gear. “How people play at home has shifted, and it is as much about relaxing and connecting with others as it is about performing, which changes what the space has to do,” said Ikea product design developer, Philip Dilé. “Together, we set out to make furniture people really want in their home, not furniture they accept because it is what you need to game.” [Image: [Image: [Image: [Image: The green X-shaped scatter cushion and thumbstick-inspired stool are among the most Xbox-coded pieces in the Yxstaby collection. Ikea says the stool was developed using original 3D design files for the Xbox controller, with the grippy textured surface now serving to prevent your butt from slipping around instead of sweaty thumbs. The lounge chair comes with a mesh pocket on the underside that’s designed to store your game controllers, but it also looks roomy enough for wider items like magazines and large books. [Image: [Image: [Image: [Image: The TV stand is an easel-style design that’s available in white or black (presumably as a nod to the Xbox console color schemes), and features shelves and hooks for holding your various gadgets and gaming accessories. It also comes with castors so it can be wheeled around the home, as does the side table, which includes a green tray for additional storage. [Image: [Image: [Image: [Image: The mirrored display box comes in black or white, and looks ideal for anyone who wants to turn a collection of Xbox gaming controllers into wall decor. The metalic trinket dish is inspired by the D-pad controller, but subtle enough to not appear obviously gaming related. There’s also a wooden toolbox, which is one of the least Xbox-coded looking items in the collection, but Ikea says it also doubles as a laptop stand for some reason. “I queued all night 25 years ago to get my hands on the first Xbox console, so those shapes are nostalgic to me,” says Ikea designer David Wahl. “The challenge was making it work as a stool, with the right seating curve and stability, while still feeling like a thumbstick. It even moves the way a thumbstick does, so it tilts with you while you play.”  Yxstaby will be available online and in Ikea stores sometime this Autumn, although prices and launch dates will vary by market.

articles.title: Fable: After Watching a Full Quest, I Couldn’t Be More Excited to Play It | gamescom 2026
articles.summary: Beer, swearing, and aggressive strangers. I feel at home. After watching a full quest from Fable, I couldn't be more excited to play it. Our preview:
articles.body:
Beer, swearing, and aggressive strangers. Just your average Thursday night in a North London pub. Turns out fantasy isn’t too far from reality, though, with a stroll around Fable delivering the exact same ingredients for an eventful afternoon. A hands-off presentation at gamescom 2026 gave me new insight into developer Playground Games’ Albion and the stories taking place in it. Here, I’ll walk you through everything that was shown, ahead of me going hands-on with Fable and its combat systems later — stay tuned for my impressions of that very soon. For now, it’s time to take a trip through Bowerstone and see what a full quest brings with it.

For those uninitiated in the original Fable trilogy, Bowerstone is the capital of the fantasy world of Albion, and it’s never looked better than it does here. At the beginning of my roughly 15-minute live gameplay demo, our hero, a young woman with a sword on her back, rode up to the portcullis of the looming city. What could be an intimidating sight quickly turned into one of awe, though, with its central keep towering over crooked, smaller buildings that stack up towards it. There’s a pleasing off-kilterness to the town, reflecting the imbalance in its world as good struggles to outweigh evil. The askew rooftops and twisty brickwork marry beautifully with the winding nature of the city’s streets and the uneven cobblestones that make them. It all makes this world feel entirely handcrafted and believably constructed by the people that live there, rather than a dull geometric pattern laid down by an unimaginative city planner.

It’s not just a sight to behold, though, but a city full of purpose. Over 30 businesses are dotted across it, from hairdressers to clothes shops to tattoo parlours. Playground really wants you to create a character entirely in your own image, and make them feel as married to the world you walk them through as possible. Speaking of marriage, our first stop in Bowerstone takes us to the hero’s family home — a cosy, well-kept cottage warmed by a roaring fireplace. Waiting for us are our daughter, Daisy, and spouse, Elliott. The love between him and our hero is still strong, it seems – as she walks away from him, he can’t help but remark, “Ooph, so glad I married all of that”. Steady on, Elliott, we’ve got a village to save.

Briar Hill is that village, and the crux of Fable’s main story. A mysterious red-cloaked figure called Isabel has turned the people of our hometown to stone, and it's up to us to reanimate them. This quest we’re on now seems fairly early on in the plot, and has taken us to the capital to gain access to the Heroes Guild. A previous mission has popped the key to the Guild’s headquarters in our inventory, and so we stroll up to the huge doors with ease. Again, both the exterior and interior architecture and art design on show are wonderful, with a delightful mix of grandeur and deliberate rough edges on show.

Sitting inside the guild is Humphry the Golden, a legendary figure in Albion folklore who appears to have seen better days. Played by Peep Show’s Super Hans supremo, Matt King, he cuts the figure of a bedraggled alcoholic, slumped in a large chair in the darkness. Never meet your heroes has never proved a truer phrase. Proving my point, in a stupor, he asks for a large beer, and we’re presented with our first choice — Playground promises Fable is packed full of both big and small decisions that will impact everything from minor character relationships to major story moments. Do you give Humphry the tankard full of hoppy goodness, or throw it over him in an attempt to wake him up? The latter is chosen, and a pop-up appears on the left of the screen letting us know that he now thinks we’re an arsehole.

Nonetheless, Humphry needs our help. In debt and on the cusp of being evicted, in order to gain his guidance, we’ll need to dig him out of a hole. It turns out that this once-respected hero gambled away the ownership rights of the guild and lost them to Slick Ronnie, a local Bowerstone gang leader. So, it’s now our job to get them back. It doesn’t take us long to get in trouble with this gang, either. One step back onto the streets and we’re faced with a trio of Ronnie’s lackeys who are bothering Billie, described by Playground as a “part-time playwright, full-time orphan.” Dialogue options are given, and an attempt to defuse the situation is made. Unfortunately, for them, violence is deemed necessary.

It’s the first opportunity for us to get a proper look at Fable’s combat, and I’m impressed. It’s always difficult to know how good a game’s action is until you get your hands on it yourself — something I’ll be doing in mere hours — but it certainly looks slick. Sweeping sword slashes are executed. A bow and arrow is fired satisfyingly with a ping into someone's head. A long electric whip is conjured and sent crashing down onto the group. A fireball is sculpted from our hero’s palms and sent blazing into a chest containing a now-unbeating heart. The flexibility on show is great to see, and it appears this won’t be an RPG that restricts your combat options depending on a strict class structure

That encounter earns us a skill point, and a fairly extensive skill tree is flashed up on screen and then closed before I have time to study it in any depth. However, I did see what the skill point was spent on: magical blades, a spell any Fable veteran will no doubt fondly remember. We’ll see in action shortly.

First, it’s time to head to a more down-on-its-luck part of town where Slick Ronnie’s hideout can be found. Of course, the trail takes us to a pub. The Poor House is Ronnie’s chosen watering hole, and after talking to its clientele, it becomes apparent we need access to the back area of the establishment. There are multiple ways in, but we choose the easy road and pay for entry to save time.

Once through the door, we find ourselves faced with another lock we don’t have the key for. This door is unguarded, however, so we put our trusty lockpicking skills to the test and gain swift entry. There’s no Fallout-esque tumbler-rotating minigame to play here, just a simple hold of a button instead. Ronnie’s office waits on the other side, and the deeds to the guild are there to be plundered. Just walking away would be far too simple, though, wouldn’t it? On the way out, Ronnie isn’t very happy to see us, and a quick attempt to bluff her by saying we wandered into this restricted area after a few too many drinks doesn’t go down well. It’s time to fight again, and the perfect opportunity for those magical blades to see some action.

Upon triggering the attack, three glowing blue swords float above our heads before darting towards an enemy each – it’s very much the spell you remember, and a good indicator that Playground has no intention of abandoning Fable’s history. It appears to be a great crowd control tool when surrounded by multiple attackers, as we are here. A follow-up arrow to one of their knees makes one satisfyingly stumble as they react to the target damage, and then met with the pointed end of our sword. Things then get a little trickier here, as a bulky brute wielding a two-handed axe enters the fight. It’s instantly noticeable how many more hits he can take, so instead it seems wise to focus on building up his stagger bar through sustained attacks so a big damage window opens. Again, I’m impressed by the fluidity of the action.

This battle signals the end of our time with Fable for now, but it's that combat that I can’t wait to get my hands on. I’m left convinced by the enjoyably British tone of the world, the range of characters that inhabit it, and the stories they’re eager to tell us. I’m left hopeful the combat matches that quality, though, and will be finding out very soon if Fable feels as slick to play as it looks. I’ll let you know very soon.
